desc:
Encoding. A singly linked list is passed to your function as an array holding the node values from head to tail; an empty array is an empty list. You may build real nodes from it first, or work on the array directly. Lists you return are given as arrays of values from head to tail.

Delete every node whose value appears anywhere in the array banned, and return the values of the remaining list from head to tail. The remaining nodes keep their original order. Several nodes in a row may need to be deleted, and so may the head.

For nums = [1,2,6,3,4,5,6] and banned = [6,4] the answer is [1,2,3,5].
hints: Deleting a node means the node before it must skip over it. The head has no node before it.
Checking a value against banned by scanning the whole array for every node is slow. Put the banned values in a hash set first.
Put a dummy node in front of the head and walk with prev and cur: if cur.val is banned, set prev.next = cur.next and do not move prev; otherwise move prev forward too.
editorial: Build a hash set from banned so each membership test is O(1). Place a dummy node before the head so that deleting the head needs no special case. Then walk the list with prev (the last kept node) and cur. A banned node is unlinked with prev.next = cur.next, and prev stays where it is, so a run of banned nodes is removed correctly. A kept node becomes the new prev.
Time is O(n + m) for a list of n nodes and m banned values; extra space is O(m) for the set. Testing each node against the raw banned array would cost O(n * m).
